p01-title.text: Goal: the average of a 0/1 label is the posterior probability

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p01-bridge.name: p01-bridge

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p01-bridge.text: Prerequisite: last unit's best prediction is the conditional mean; this page asks what it is when the target is only 0 or 1.

p01-ctx-t.name: p01-ctx-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p01-ctx-t.text: **Used on this page**: conditional mean $m(\mathbf{x})=E[y\mid\mathbf{x}]$; class indicator $y_i$; posterior $p_i(\mathbf{x})=P(\omega_i\mid\mathbf{x})$.

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p01-c2-t.name: p01-c2-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p01-c2-t.text:
Learning goals: show an indicator label's conditional mean equals the posterior; split the multiclass squared loss; explain why a linear MSE score may not be a valid probability
In one line: squared loss's theoretical target is the posterior, but finite data and restricted models do not guarantee recovering it exactly
A detective notes only whether a class appears each time; averaging under the same conditions estimates that class's share

p01-ban-t.name: p01-ban-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p01-ban-t.text: Takeaway: encode classes as 0 and 1, and the best squared-error prediction is the probability.

p02-title.name: p02-title

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p02-title.text: Classes as indicators: 1 if in the class, 0 if not; the mean is the probability

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p02-bridge.name: p02-bridge

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p02-bridge.text: Last page: the target is only 0 or 1. This page uses an indicator variable to find its conditional mean.

p02-ctx-t.name: p02-ctx-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p02-ctx-t.text: **Used on this page**: $y_i=\mathbf{1}\{\omega=\omega_i\}$; $M$ exclusive classes, one 1 in the target; $p_i=P(\omega_i\mid\mathbf{x})$.

p02-fig-title.name: p02-fig-title

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p02-fig-title.text: One sample's target vector has a single 1

p02-c2-t.name: p02-c2-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p02-c2-t.text:
$E[y_i\mid\mathbf{x}]=1\,p_i(\mathbf{x})+0\,[1-p_i(\mathbf{x})]=p_i(\mathbf{x})$
This is an identity for random variables
It needs no Gaussian assumption on the feature density, and no prior estimate of each class's density

p02-ban-t.name: p02-ban-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p02-ban-t.text: Takeaway: the conditional mean of a 0/1 indicator is exactly the posterior probability.

p03-title.name: p03-title

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-title.text: Squared loss: distance from the probability plus the 0/1 spread

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-bridge.name: p03-bridge

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-bridge.text: Last page: the mean is the probability. This page applies last unit's split to squared loss.

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-fig-title.name: p03-fig-title

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-fig-title.text: Two terms: an approximation term that can reach zero, and a fixed term that cannot

p03-c2-t.name: p03-c2-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-c2-t.text:
At a fixed input, split each label: $E[(g_i-y_i)^2\mid\mathbf{x}]=(g_i-p_i)^2+p_i(1-p_i)$
The second term is the 0/1 variable's conditional variance, independent of the prediction function
Sum over classes and average over inputs to get J's two terms

p03-ban-t.name: p03-ban-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-ban-t.text: Takeaway: the model can only reduce the first term; the fixed term is the class's own uncertainty, which cannot be removed.

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-fl0-b.name: p03-fl0-b

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p03-fl0-b.text:
$E\left[\sum_i(g_i-p_i)^2\right]$
can be zero with no function limit

p03-bx1-t.text:
With only linear functions allowed, we find the solution in that family closest to the posterior
[Added] The fixed term can also be written $E[1-\sum_ip_i^2]$: class uncertainty leaves squared loss

p04-title.name: p04-title

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p04-title.text: Eight to two: predicting 0.8 has risk 0.16, while predicting 1 gives 0.20

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p04-bridge.name: p04-bridge

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p04-bridge.text: Last page: the two-term split. This page compares two predictions on ten records using $p_1(x_0)=0.8$.

p04-ctx-t.name: p04-ctx-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p04-ctx-t.text: **Used on this page**: $x_0=2$, $p_1=0.8$; of ten records 8 are 1 and 2 are 0; $\hat R(g)=\frac{8(g-1)^2+2g^2}{10}$.

p04-fig-title.name: p04-fig-title

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p04-fig-title.text: Mean squared loss of two predictions

p04-c2-t.name: p04-c2-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p04-c2-t.text:
$\bar y=\frac{8(1)+2(0)}{10}=0.8$: the sample share equals the assumed probability here; a typical draw's 8/10 is only an estimate
Predicting 1 seems more confident, yet the squared loss rises by $0.04=(1-0.8)^2$
The aim is not to output the right class each time, but to reflect the class uncertainty under the same conditions

p04-ban-t.name: p04-ban-t

style.fontFamily: "Microsoft JhengHei", "Noto Sans CJK TC", "PingFang TC", "Segoe UI", sans-serif

p04-ban-t.text: Takeaway: the smallest squared loss comes from reporting probability 0.8, not 1.

Finite data and restricted models do not guarantee recovering the posterior exactly
